entities.name: Mamie Phipps Clark
entities.description: Dr. Mamie Phipps Clark (1917-1983) was a pioneering African American social psychologist whose groundbreaking research on racial identity and child development played a crucial role in the landmark Brown v. Board of Education Supreme Court case. Born in Hot Springs, Arkansas, she became the first Black woman to earn a Ph.D. in psychology from Columbia University in 1943. Her most famous contribution was the doll study, which demonstrated that African American children as young as three developed negative self-images and preferred white dolls over black ones due to segregation and societal prejudice. This research provided the first social science evidence ever presented to the Supreme Court and was instrumental in ending school segregation. Despite facing significant discrimination as a Black woman in a white-dominated field, Clark co-founded the Northside Center for Child Development in 1946, the first organization in New York City to provide mental health services to African American children, which she directed until her retirement in 1979. Her work spanned over three decades and fundamentally changed both the field of psychology and the course of civil rights in America.

entities.description: [Model Material: Wax] Published on September 6, 2023, by Scotland and Medicine, this 4-minute read blog post explores the historical use of wax in anatomical teaching, detailing how the University of St Andrews' Anatomy and Pathology Collection contains over 90 wax and plaster models purchased from companies like Tramond of Paris and Fredrick Ziegler of Germany between 1900-1910. The article explains that wax models were developed due to cadaver shortages and preservation challenges, with dissection in Scotland limited to winter months, and highlights dermatological wax moulages, including a 1925 model of Boeck's sarcoid created by Miss Rae in Edinburgh based on patient Mrs Fisher's condition. The post references the world's first dermatological wax moulage museum, opened in Paris in 1867, and mentions conservation challenges like wax bloom affecting these fragile artifacts.

entities.name: Munich's Lenbachhaus Museum Faces Critical Shortage of Fluorescent Tubes for Dan Flavin's Light Art Installation
entities.description: This Sayart news article from August 20, 2025, reports on the Lenbachhaus Museum in Munich confronting an unprecedented conservation challenge with Dan Flavin's monumental light installation "For Ksenija" (1994). The installation features approximately 300 fluorescent tubes in green, blue, yellow, and pink colors spanning the 110-meter Kunstbau underground gallery. The specific fluorescent tubes required are no longer available for purchase due to EU environmental regulations targeting energy consumption and mercury content. Curator Johannes Stanislaus and restorer Isabel Gebhardt detail how Flavin's artistic philosophy of using commercially available 1990s products now creates a preservation dilemma. The museum faces critical questions about supply sufficiency and potential solutions, with any modification requiring approval from Dan Flavin's estate representatives in New York. This conservation crisis affects works by other deceased light artists including François Morellet, Keith Sonnier, and Mario Merz, highlighting broader challenges in preserving contemporary art dependent on obsolete industrial components.

entities.name: James Marion Sims
entities.description: James Marion Sims (1813-1883) was an American surgeon who pioneered a surgical technique for repairing vesicovaginal fistula, a devastating childbirth injury. He developed this method through a series of experimental surgeries performed between 1845 and 1849 on enslaved Black women, primarily Anarcha Westcott, Lucy, and Betsey, who were unable to give consent and often operated on without anesthesia. Sims also invented several medical instruments that bear his name, including the Sims speculum, the Sims sigmoid catheter, and the Sims position, and he founded the Woman's Hospital in New York in 1855. Once celebrated as the "father of modern gynecology" and honored with the first U.S. statue of a physician in 1894, his legacy is now highly controversial due to his unethical human experimentation, leading to the removal of his Central Park statue in 2018 and widespread condemnation from modern medical ethicists.

entities.name: Daiei Film (大映映画株式会社)
entities.description: Daiei Film Co., Ltd. was a major Japanese film studio founded in 1942 during World War II through the government-mandated merger of Shinkō Kinema, Daito Eiga, and Nikkatsu's production arm. Originally named Dai Nippon Film Co., Ltd., it became a powerhouse during the postwar Golden Age of Japanese cinema, producing internationally acclaimed masterpieces such as Akira Kurosawa's Rashomon (1950)—the first Japanese film to win an international award—and Kenji Mizoguchi's Ugetsu (1953). Beyond art-house classics, Daiei created enduring genre franchises including the Zatoichi series, the Gamera kaiju films, the Daimajin trilogy, and the Yokai Monsters series. The studio declared bankruptcy in 1971 due to financial mismanagement and declining attendance, was briefly revived by Tokuma Shoten in 1974, and was ultimately merged into Kadokawa Pictures in 2002, with its legacy continuing through Kadokawa Daiei Studio.

entities.name: Ben Laposky's Oscillons
entities.description: This academic blog post from the Computer Arts Society archives is an excerpt from Nick Lambert's PhD thesis "A critical examination of 'computer art'" (2009). The article provides a comprehensive analysis of Ben Laposky's pioneering "Oscillons" work from the 1950s, explaining how he used oscilloscopes to create what are considered the first computer graphics. Laposky's method involved feeding sine waves into horizontal and vertical amplifiers to generate complex Lissajous figures, with some pieces requiring up to 70 different control settings. The text emphasizes how Laposky's work marked a crucial transition between traditional art forms and computer art, highlighting the unique qualities of electronic images that were "insubstantial," often moving, and could only be achieved through primitive computer technology. The article includes technical details about Laposky's custom-built instruments and his use of colored phosphors, noting that the results were seldom replicable due to the analog nature of his computing methods.

entities.name: Papal State Silver Lira Coins (里拉银器)
entities.description: The Papal State Silver Lira coins from the 1860s are rare historical artifacts that represent the monetary system of the Papal States, territories under direct papal rule from 756 to 1870. These genuine silver coins depict Pope Pius IX (1792-1878), who had the longest papal reign in history at 32 years, and were minted during a period when the Pope held both spiritual and temporal power over central Italian territories. The coins serve as tangible links to the era when the Papal States encompassed Vatican City and various central Italian regions, representing a unique fusion of faith, governance, and historical intrigue. Currently valued at $602.00, these artifacts come with certificates of authenticity and protective display cases, and are primarily sourced from European collections and recovered hoards throughout Italy. The broader category of Italian silver lira coins includes various denominations minted from 1861-1917 (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, and 50 lire coins) and later 500 lire silver coins from 1958-2001, with some rare specimens valued at thousands of euros depending on their condition, rarity, and historical significance.

entities.name: Institute of Brewing and Distilling
entities.description: The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) is the world's leading professional body for brewers, distillers, and allied professionals, originally established as The Laboratory Club in 1886 by ten scientists interested in malting and brewing science. The organization evolved through several mergers, becoming the Institute of Brewing around 1895, then the Institute and Guild of Brewing in 2001 after merging with the Brewers' Guild, and finally the Institute of Brewing and Distilling in 2005. In 2023, the IBD was granted Royal Charter status and transitioned to become the Chartered Institute of Brewers and Distillers (CIBD) on January 1, 2025. Headquartered in London, the institute moved from Clarges Street to Curlew Street in 2014 and serves an international community across 90 countries, offering comprehensive qualifications from Foundation to Masters level in brewing, distilling, packaging, malting, and cider making. The IBD publishes the Journal of the Institute of Brewing and The Brewer and Distiller International magazine, maintaining its mission to advance education and professional development in brewing and distilling science and technology since its inception when there were nearly 20,000 licensed breweries in the UK.

entities.name: Printing and Protestants: Reforming the Economics of the Reformation
entities.description: This 2011 academic paper by Jared Rubin from California State University, Fullerton, presents an econometric analysis testing the causal relationship between the spread of the printing press and the Protestant Reformation. Using city-level data from the Holy Roman Empire, Rubin finds that cities within 10 miles of a printing press by 1500 were 57.4 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600, even after controlling for various city characteristics. The paper argues that the printing press permitted Reformation ideas to reach broader audiences, making it the first major historical movement facilitated by this new information technology. The analysis suggests the early spread of press affected religious choice patterns well into the 19th century, and the findings remain robust across Western Europe, though with weaker effects.

entities.name: Eoscyphella luciurceolata gen. and sp. nov. (Agaricomycetes) Shed Light on Cyphellopsidaceae with a New Lineage of Bioluminescent Fungi
entities.description: Published on October 12, 2023, in the Journal of Fungi, this groundbreaking scientific paper describes Eoscyphella luciurceolata, a completely new genus and species of bioluminescent fungus discovered during nocturnal expeditions in Brazil's Atlantic Rainforest. The research team, led by Alexandre G. S. Silva-Filho and involving 11 international scientists, conducted phylogenetic analyses using ITS rDNA and LSU rDNA sequences to confirm this represents the first bioluminescent member of the Cyphellopsidaceae family. The fungus is characterized by its unique vasiform to urceolate basidiomata, subglobose to broadly ellipsoid basidiospores, and the absence of conspicuous external hairs, making it morphologically distinct from all known bioluminescent species. This discovery is particularly significant as it represents only the second lineage of bioluminescent fungi with reduced forms and contributes to the recent doubling of known bioluminescent fungal species from 64 to 132 over the past 15 years.

entities.name: Ibn Yunus
entities.description: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi al-Said 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn Yunus ibn Abd al-'Ala al-Sadafi al-Misri (c. 950 - 1009) was an Egyptian astronomer and mathematician who worked for the Fatimid dynasty in Cairo for twenty-six years, serving under Caliphs al-Aziz Billah and al-Hakim. His most famous work, the al-Zij al-Kabir al-Hakimi, was a monumental astronomical handbook containing 81 chapters with over 34,000 entries for lunar position calculations and remarkably accurate observations of 40 planetary conjunctions and 30 lunar eclipses. Ibn Yunus was the first to establish a law for spherical trigonometry that converted multiplication operations into addition operations, facilitating complex astronomical calculations before the discovery of logarithms. His astronomical observations were so precise that they were later used by Richard Dunthorne and Simon Newcomb in their calculations of the secular acceleration of the Moon. Known as an eccentric, absent-minded man who dressed shabbily, Ibn Yunus famously predicted the exact date of his own death seven days in advance, locked himself in his house, and died on the predicted day while reciting the Quran.

entities.description: [Sonic restoration: Acoustic stimulation enhances soil fungal biomass and activity of plant growth-promoting fungi] This pre-print study from Flinders University, published on bioRxiv in January 2024, investigates how sound waves affect soil fungi growth. Researchers exposed Trichoderma harzianum fungus to 8 kHz frequency sound at 80 decibels for up to 8 hours daily over 14 days, finding that spore activity increased five-fold compared to control groups. The experiment used teabags buried in soundproof boxes to measure biomass growth, with treated samples gaining approximately 0.5g more fungal biomass than controls. Led by microbial ecologist Dr. Jake Robinson, the research suggests "eco-acoustics" could revolutionize ecosystem restoration, potentially accelerating soil recovery which normally takes decades after revegetation. The study notes that over 75% of world soils are degraded, positioning sound stimulation as a radical new approach to restoring biodiversity and supporting food production.

It covers applications in visual design (high contrast increases positive evaluations by Reber et al., 2004), naming (difficult-to-pronounce names are judged more harmful per Song & Schwarz, 2009), and messaging (concrete language boosts perceived truthfulness per Hansen & Wänke, 2010). The post includes a 5-step action plan and notes that fluency-focused testing outperforms feature-focused testing by 23% according to Widerfunnel.

entities.name: Samuel "Sam" Israel III
entities.description: Samuel "Sam" Israel III (born July 20, 1959) is an American former hedge fund manager and convicted fraudster who orchestrated one of Wall Street's most notorious Ponzi schemes through his Bayou Hedge Fund Group, which he founded in 1996. Israel, who came from a wealthy New Orleans commodities trading family, raised $450 million from investors but misappropriated funds and created a dummy accounting firm to hide massive losses, ultimately defrauding victims out of approximately $300 million. After pleading guilty in 2008 and receiving a 20-year prison sentence, Israel famously attempted to fake his own death by abandoning his SUV on the Bear Mountain Bridge with "Suicide is Painless" written on the hood, leading to a month-long manhunt before his capture. Currently incarcerated at FCI Butner Low with a scheduled release date of May 10, 2026, Israel's case exemplifies the excesses of the "new gilded age" and remains a cautionary tale in financial crime history.

entities.name: Musée du cinéma Henri-Langlois
entities.description: The Musée du cinéma Henri-Langlois was inaugurated in 1972 at the Palais de Chaillot by Henri Langlois, founder of the Cinémathèque française. This pioneering museum showcased over 5,000 cinema artifacts, including cameras, scripts, and costumes worn by legends like Marilyn Monroe and Rudolph Valentino. In 1997, a fire at the neighboring Museum of French Monuments forced the museum's evacuation, leading to a landmark court ruling that protected it as "the creative work of one man." The museum was relocated in 2005 to Frank Gehry's former American Center at 51 rue de Bercy, where it merged with the Cinémathèque and Bibliothèque du film to form the modern Musée de la Cinémathèque.

entities.name: 'Bug Wrangler' Scratches Filmdom's Itch for Insects
entities.description: Published on March 6, 1988, in the Los Angeles Times, this article profiles Steven R. Kutcher, a 44-year-old entomologist and Hollywood "bug wrangler" who has provided insects for over 100 films. Kutcher, who holds a Master's degree in insect behavior from California State University, Long Beach, maintains a collection of 3,000 live insects and has worked on productions like 'The Terminator' and 'Spider-Man'. The article reveals he once caught 1,100 butterflies in three hours for a wedding scene and provided 40,000 carpenter ants for a single film. Despite feeding Hollywood's entomophobia through horror films, Kutcher uses his entertainment income to fund educational programs, where his pet tarantula Dolores has helped 8,000 schoolchildren overcome their fear of insects. He teaches biology at two community colleges and advocates for insect conservation, warning that depleting insect populations threatens entire food chains.

entities.name: Ettore Majorana
entities.description: Ettore Majorana (1906-1938) was an Italian theoretical physicist whose brilliance was compared by Enrico Fermi to Galileo and Newton. Born in Catania, Sicily, he joined Fermi's "Via Panisperna boys" at age 22 and published only nine papers before his mysterious disappearance at age 31. His most significant contributions include the Majorana equation predicting particles that are their own antiparticles (Majorana fermions), work on exchange forces, and early insights into neutron discovery. Despite publishing so little, his work was decades ahead of its time - his neutrino mass theories are now central to particle physics and quantum computing research. On March 25, 1938, after withdrawing his life savings and boarding a ship from Naples to Palermo, he vanished without a trace, leaving behind one of science's greatest unsolved mysteries. Theories range from suicide to voluntary disappearance to political abduction, but no definitive evidence has ever been found. His legacy lives on through the Majorana Prize (established in 2006), the Majorana Demonstrator project for neutrino research, and Microsoft's Majorana 1 quantum computing device.

entities.name: blog_post
entities.description: [The tales emergency currency can tell] This Smithsonian blog post, published on October 29, 2020, by collections specialist Alisha Ankin, explores German Notgeld (emergency currency) from the Harz mountains featuring Walpurgisnacht witch themes. The article specifically details a 25 pfennig note from Brocken, Germany, issued in 1921, which depicts witches flying to meet with the Devil on Walpurgis Night. The note illustrates local folklore including landmarks like Hexentanzplatz (Witches' Dance Floor), Teufelsmauer (Devil's Wall), and Hexenaltar (Witches' Altar). The post explains how during the post-WWI economic crisis, German towns issued highly illustrated emergency currency featuring local legends, with the Brocken note showing how folklore provided messages of comfort during uncertainty. The article is approximately 800 words and includes four examples of Notgeld with different folklore themes.

entities.name: The Curious History of the Republic of Rose Island, a Micronation on a Man-Made Platform off the Coast of Italy
entities.description: This comprehensive blog post by Matteo Damiani details the fascinating story of Italian engineer Giorgio Rosa's 1968 micronation project. The article covers the complete timeline from construction beginning in 1958 to demolition in 1969, including technical specifications of the 400m² platform supported by nine pylons positioned 11.6km off Rimini's coast. Key details include Rose Island's declaration of independence on May 1, 1968, its adoption of Esperanto as the official language (Respubliko de la Insulo de la Rozoj), creation of currency called "Mill" (Milo in Esperanto), and amenities including restaurant, bar, nightclub, souvenir shop, and post office. The article provides extensive information about the Italian government's response, including naval blockade, occupation on June 26, 1968, and eventual demolition using 675kg of explosives on February 11, 1969, followed by a final 1080kg explosion attempt before the structure finally sank during a storm on February 26, 1969. The post includes an FAQ section addressing location, destruction reasons, official language, and current visitation status, along with biographical information about Rosa who lived to age 92, dying in March 2017.

entities.name: Mycena lamprocephala, a new luminescent species from the Brazilian Amazon
entities.description: Published on January 18, 2024, in Phytotaxa (Vol. 634, No. 3, pp. 187-203), this peer-reviewed paper by Célia C.B. Soares et al. describes Mycena lamprocephala sp. nov., a newly discovered bioluminescent fungus from the Brazilian Amazon. The species was collected in terra-firme forest at the upper Cuieiras river in Amazonas, Brazil, and is characterized by small, thin basidiomata with an olivaceous brown pileus and glutinous stipe. Microscopically, it features diverticulate pleurocystidia, ramose cheilocystidia, and thin, diverticulate pileipellis hyphae. The fungus emits typically green luminescence from both its pileus and mycelium, which can sometimes appear pulsating. This discovery represents the third luminescent species of Mycenaceae described from the Amazon Forest and is supported by phylogenetic analysis using ITS+LSU data. The 24.19MB PDF has been downloaded 836 times and viewed abstractly 1,168 times as of the publication date.

entities.name: CRIME: The Fabulous Hoax of Clifford Irving
entities.description: This TIME magazine article from February 21, 1972, provides a comprehensive 24-minute investigation into Clifford Irving's elaborate hoax to publish a fake autobiography of reclusive billionaire Howard Hughes. The article reveals how Irving convinced McGraw-Hill to pay $765,000 ($650,000 for Hughes, $100,000 for himself) for the fraudulent manuscript, with Life magazine purchasing excerpt rights. TIME's investigation uncovered that Irving's "autobiography" was largely plagiarized from James Phelan's manuscript about Noah Dietrich, Hughes's former chief of staff. The piece details how Irving created forged documents, fabricated meetings with Hughes, and maintained the deception until TIME discovered the plagiarism by comparing Irving's manuscript with Phelan's work. The article includes specific details about the Swiss bank accounts where Irving's wife Edith deposited the Hughes checks, the involvement of handwriting experts who initially authenticated the forgeries, and the legal negotiations that led to Irving's eventual confession to federal prosecutors.

entities.name: First word discovered in unopened Herculaneum scroll by 21yo computer...
entities.description: This official Vesuvius Challenge announcement from October 12, 2023, details how Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old computer science student from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, became the first person in 2,000 years to read an entire word from within an unopened Herculaneum scroll using artificial intelligence. Farritor won the $40,000 First Letters Prize for discovering the ancient Greek word "πορϕυρας" (porphyras), meaning "purple," by training a machine learning model to detect subtle "crackle patterns" in CT scans of the carbonized papyrus. The scroll was one of hundreds buried and carbonized by Mount Vesuvius' eruption in 79 AD, representing the only intact library to survive from Greco-Roman antiquity. Shortly after Farritor's breakthrough, Youssef Nader independently confirmed the same discovery using a different machine learning approach, winning a $10,000 second-place prize. The achievement built on Casey Handmer's earlier discovery of ink evidence, which earned him a $10,000 First Ink Prize. The competition offers a grand prize of $700,000 for reading four passages of at least 140 characters from the ancient scrolls.

entities.name: A peculiar object in Serpens
entities.description: This groundbreaking 1950 paper by Arthur A. Hoag, published in The Astronomical Journal (Volume 55, No. 1186), documents the first discovery of what would later become known as Hoag's Object. Hoag discovered this unusual celestial object on a 75-minute exposure using a Jewett Schmidt photographic plate, describing it as appearing to be a perfectly symmetrical planetary nebula with a perfect halo of 17 arc seconds in radius surrounding a diffuse central image. The object's position was recorded as 15h 15m 0s, +21° 46' (1950 coordinates) with galactic coordinates l=358°, b=+54°. Hoag noted that the object's characteristics were not typical of planetary nebulae - the halo was bluer than the nucleus and did not show emission on an objective prism plate that recorded the central object. He proposed that as a most conservative alternative, this might represent a new species among "pathological" galaxies, while considering other ring-forming mechanisms like diffraction effects or gravitational lensing as less probable explanations. In the gravitational lensing scenario, Hoag calculated that the central object would need a mass of approximately 8 × 10^11 solar masses. Recognizing the uniqueness of his discovery, Hoag concluded by suggesting that proper identification would be a worthwhile short-term project for the astronomical community. This seminal work established the foundation for decades of research into this rare type of ring galaxy.

entities.name: Population Density and Social Pathology
entities.description: Published in Scientific American in February 1962 by ethologist John B. Calhoun, this landmark paper documents the foundational experiments that led to the concept of the "behavioral sink." The study involved observing six populations of domesticated Norway rats confined in 10-by-14-foot rooms divided into four pens, each designed to support 12 adults comfortably. Despite abundant resources and the absence of predators or disease, the populations grew to 80 adults, leading to severe behavioral pathologies. The paper reports that infant mortality reached catastrophic levels—as high as 96% in the most disoriented groups—due to the complete breakdown of maternal behavior. Calhoun documented how rats would crowd into a single pen, creating a pathological aggregation where up to 60 of 80 rats would eat together, transforming vital biological activities into destructive social interactions that ultimately led to the populations' functional extinction.

entities.name: System Development Corporation
entities.description: System Development Corporation (SDC) was a pioneering computer software company based in Santa Monica, California, founded in December 1955 as a division of the RAND Corporation and established as an independent organization in October 1956. Considered the world's first computer software company, SDC began as the systems engineering group for the SAGE air-defense system and quickly grew from 500 to 1,000 employees within its first year. The organization was so influential in training programmers that it was referred to as "a university for programmers" and trained a large portion of the emerging programmer workforce in the United States during the late 1950s. SDC developed several groundbreaking technologies including the first computerized encyclopedia in 1964, the JOVIAL programming language, and the Time-Shared Data Management System (TDMS). The company underwent multiple ownership transitions throughout its history, being sold to Burroughs Corporation in 1981, eventually becoming part of Unisys, and later evolving through Paramax, Loral, Lockheed Martin, and L-3 Communications before becoming part of L3Harris Technologies in 2019.

entities.name: Saudi Consolidated Electric Company, Western Province (SCECO West)
entities.description: Saudi Consolidated Electric Company, Western Province (SCECO West) was one of four regional electricity companies established in Saudi Arabia between 1976 and 1981 to consolidate and manage the country's decentralized power generation systems. SCECO West was responsible for electricity generation, transmission, and distribution in the Western Province, which includes major cities like Jeddah and Mecca. By 1990, the Western Province's electricity infrastructure served millions of subscribers, with industry accounting for over 60% of consumption in some regions due to major industrial complexes. The company operated under local ownership until the formation of the Saudi Electricity Company in 2000, which eventually merged all regional SCECOs into a national monopoly. SCECO West's headquarters were in Makkah, and it played a critical role in electrifying the holy cities and supporting industrial growth in the region during the late 20th century.

entities.name: Janus Films
entities.description: Founded in 1956 by Bryant Haliday and Cyrus Harvey, Jr., at the Brattle Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Janus Films is the oldest and most respected American distributor dedicated to international art-house cinema. The company is credited with introducing U.S. audiences to master filmmakers like Ingmar Bergman, Federico Fellini, Akira Kurosawa, and Andrei Tarkovsky, with Ingmar Bergman's *The Seventh Seal* being the film that launched its initial success. Now headquartered in New York City and owned by Steven Rales since 2024, Janus manages a library of over 1,200 films and maintains a close partnership with The Criterion Collection for home video releases. After a 30-year hiatus from first-run theatrical distribution, the company re-entered the market with films like *Revanche* (2009) and achieved its highest-grossing release ever with the Academy Award-winning animated film *Flow* (2024).

entities.name: blog_post
entities.description: [Caveat Lecter: Good news for fans of anthropodermic bibliopegy, bibliomaniacs and cannibals alike] Published in June 2014 by Harvard's Houghton Library, this now-infamous blog post announced the scientific confirmation that "Des destinées de l'âme" was bound in human skin through a practice called anthropodermic bibliopegy. The post's provocative title and flippant tone—which included references to "fans of anthropodermic bibliopegy, bibliomaniacs and cannibals alike"—sparked international media coverage and was later criticized by the library itself as sensationalistic. The scientific testing involved analyzing proteins using mass spectrometry, which revealed that the binding was definitively human rather than sheepskin, as two other suspected books in Harvard's collections turned out to be. The blog post has since been removed from public view, with Harvard later apologizing for its "morbid and humorous tone" that further objectified the anonymous woman whose skin was used without consent in the 19th century.

entities.name: Creating a New Kind of Night Light: Glow-in-the-Dark Trees
entities.description: This Smithsonian article, published on July 10, 2013, details the ambitious Kickstarter campaign by San Francisco entrepreneur Antony Evans and his team to engineer glow-in-the-dark trees. The project successfully raised $484,013 from 8,433 backers to fund the insertion of bioluminescent genes from marine bacteria Vibrio fischeri into Arabidopsis thaliana plants. The piece explains the technical process using Genome Compiler software and Agrobacterium, while noting that initial light output would be comparable to glow-in-the-dark paint. Evans estimates a mature glowing tree covering 1,000 square feet could match a streetlight's illumination, though he acknowledges trees present long-term experimental challenges compared to faster-growing plants.

entities.name: Haffkine Institute for Training, Research and Testing
entities.description: The Haffkine Institute for Training, Research and Testing is a historic biomedical research institution located in Parel, Mumbai, India, established on August 10, 1899 by Dr. Waldemar Mordechai Haffkine as the "Plague Research Laboratory" [0, 1]. Originally founded to combat the bubonic plague epidemic, the institute pioneered the world's first effective plague vaccine when Haffkine tested it on himself on January 10, 1897 [0, 2]. The institute is housed in the Sans Pareil mansion, which was once the official residence of the governor of Bombay and was originally built as a Jesuit chapel in 1673 [0]. Over its 112+ year history, the institute evolved from a bacteriology research center into a multi-disciplinary biomedical research organization conducting studies in bacteriology, virology, zoonosis, biochemistry, toxicology, chemotherapy, and clinical pathology [1, 3]. Currently affiliated with the University of Mumbai for M.Sc and Ph.D. programs, the institute has been at the forefront of recent public health emergencies, testing over 55,000 COVID-19 samples and serving as the nodal laboratory for influenza surveillance programs [3]. The institute received ISO 9001:2008 certification in 2012 and opened a museum in March 2014 to showcase its microbiological research and history [0].

entities.description: The Museum of Jurassic Technology, located at 9341 Venice Boulevard in Culver City, California, is a unique educational institution founded in 1988 by David Hildebrand Wilson and Diana Drake Wilson. It presents itself as dedicated to the advancement of knowledge and public appreciation of the Lower Jurassic, though its exhibits blur the lines between fact and fiction, science and art. The museum features permanent collections such as Hagop Sandaldjian's microminiature sculptures—some as small as a micron, requiring the artist to work between heartbeats to avoid accidental destruction. Other notable exhibits include micromosaics by Harold Henry Dalton and the "Tell The Bees" installation exploring hypersymbolic cognition. The institution operates with dim atmospheric lighting and requires advance ticket reservations, embodying its enigmatic, immersive approach to knowledge.

entities.name: Eustace Hamilton Miles
entities.description: Eustace Hamilton Miles (1868-1948) was an English real tennis champion who won the Olympic silver medal in Jeu de Paume at the 1908 London Games, losing to American Jay Gould II whom he had previously coached. He dominated the English Amateur Real Tennis Championship, winning it nine times between 1898-1910, and was the first non-American to win the US Real Tennis Championship in 1900. Beyond sports, Miles was a prolific author of over 20 books including "The Game of Squash" (1901), the first book ever written about squash, and became a prominent health and diet reformer who established the Eustace Miles Restaurant in London and created his own health food product called "Emprote." Despite his early success and influence in both sports and health reform, Miles eventually went bankrupt and died in 1948 leaving only £175.

entities.name: #ResearchNote - Project Suntan: The Huge Hydrogen Aircraft That Might Have Blown Up Southern California
entities.description: Published on August 23, 2023, by Dr. Michael W. Hankins (Curator for US Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps post-World War II Aviation at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum), this article reveals the hidden history of Project Suntan—a 1956-1958 top-secret US Air Force and Lockheed program to build a liquid hydrogen-powered spyplane to succeed the U-2. The CL-400 aircraft design evolved to massive proportions: the original was 160 feet long (near the size of a B-52), while later variants like the CL-400-13 reached nearly a football field in length with a 376,000-pound takeoff weight and Mach 4 cruising capability. Most remarkably, the article details Lockheed's secret hydrogen safety experiments near Burbank Airport, where engineers deliberately tried to cause hydrogen explosions 61 times to prove the fuel's safety—only achieving bona fide explosions twice when mixing hydrogen with oxygen. The project was ultimately cancelled due to insurmountable logistical challenges, but its design innovations directly influenced later aircraft like the A-12 and SR-71 Blackbird.

entities.name: Measurement of the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux over six seasons using cascade events from the Baikal-GVD expanding telescope
entities.description: This arXiv preprint (arXiv:2507.01893v2), submitted on July 2, 2025, and revised on July 9, 2025, presents the Baikal-GVD Collaboration's analysis of neutrino flux data collected from April 2018 to March 2024 in Lake Baikal, Russia. During this six-year period, the deep underwater detector expanded from 15% to 55% of its planned cubic-kilometer configuration, enabling the detection of diffuse astrophysical neutrinos with 5.1σ statistical significance. The paper reports key findings: under flavor equipartition assumptions (νe:νμ:ντ ≈ 1:1:1) due to neutrino oscillations over cosmic distances, the best-fit spectral index is γastro = 2.64 (+0.09/-0.11), and the flux normalization is φastro = 4.42 (+2.31/-1.29) × 10⁻¹⁸ GeV⁻¹cm⁻²s⁻¹sr⁻¹ per flavor at 100 TeV. Authored by 68 researchers from institutions across Russia, Slovakia, and the Czech Republic, this 26-page technical document includes detailed methodology on cascade event selection and background rejection, with results consistent with IceCube measurements.

entities.name: Frédéric Joliot-Curie
entities.description: Jean Frédéric Joliot-Curie (1900–1958) was a French chemist and physicist who, alongside his wife Irène Joliot-Curie, won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering induced radioactivity. By bombarding boron, aluminum, and magnesium with alpha particles, they produced short-lived radioactive isotopes like nitrogen-13 and phosphorus-30, revolutionizing nuclear medicine and physics. Joliot-Curie later oversaw the construction of France’s first atomic reactor (1948) and was a prominent political activist, leading the French Resistance during WWII and serving as the first High Commissioner for Atomic Energy. He died in 1958 from liver disease attributed to radiation exposure. His legacy includes the Orsay Faculty of Sciences and the lunar crater Joliot named in his honor.

entities.name: Tensor Product Variable Binding and the Representation of Symbolic Structures in Connectionist Systems
entities.description: This seminal 1990 paper by Paul Smolensky introduces tensor product representations (TPRs) as a general method for representing value-variable bindings in connectionist systems. Published in Artificial Intelligence (Volume 46, Issues 1-2, pages 159-216), the paper formalizes the idea that sets of value-variable pairs can be represented by accumulating activity in units that compute the product of a variable feature and its value feature. The method enables fully distributed representation of symbolic structures, allowing roles and fillers to be arbitrarily non-local. The technique supports recursive construction of complex representations, extends naturally to continuous structures, permits values to serve as variables, and enables analysis of interference in associative memories. The paper has been cited over 213 times and served as the foundation for working connectionist models of high-level cognitive tasks. The core mechanism involves role-filler binding where roles represent positions/slots in structures (like subject, verb, object) and fillers are the specific entities occupying those roles, combined through tensor products to preserve both elements and their structural relationships.

entities.name: ART REVIEW; It's a Leonardo? It's a Corot? Well, No, It's Chocolate Syrup
entities.description: Published on September 25, 1998, by Vicki Goldberg in The New York Times, this article reviews Vik Muniz's groundbreaking exhibition at the International Center of Photography Midtown. It provides an in-depth analysis of Muniz's chocolate syrup recreation of Leonardo da Vinci's "The Last Supper," noting it as "probably a first" in art history. The piece describes Muniz's ephemeral creation made with Bosco chocolate syrup—so impermanent that the artist reportedly sometimes eats his works before photographing them. The review contextualizes the artwork within Muniz's broader practice of "photographic delusions," where he uses unconventional materials (dirt, sugar, wire, thread) to recreate famous images, then photographs them to preserve the transient compositions. The exhibition featured approximately 100 images from the last decade, including other notable works like "The Best of Life" series, where Muniz drew iconic photographs from memory and printed them through a half-tone screen. The article emphasizes Muniz's playful approach to visual perception, comparing his philosophical underpinnings to Jean Baudrillard appearing "in a Hawaiian shirt," and highlights the artist's statement that he aims to create "the worst possible illusion that will still fool the eyes of the average person." The review also includes technical details about the artwork's triptych format and its inspiration from Andy Warhol's appropriations of "The Last Supper."

entities.name: The Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI)
entities.description: The NSF AI Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI, pronounced /aɪ-faɪ/) is one of the inaugural institutes established under the U.S. National Science Foundation's National Artificial Intelligence Research Institutes program. Founded in 2020, IAIFI is a collaboration between physics and AI researchers from MIT, Harvard, Northeastern, and Tufts universities, anchored in MIT's Laboratory for Nuclear Science. The institute's mission is to advance physics knowledge—from subatomic particles to cosmic structures—and galvanize AI innovation by developing novel AI approaches that incorporate first principles from fundamental physics. IAIFI's research spans four domains: foundational AI, theoretical physics, experimental physics, and astrophysics, organized around cross-cutting themes including Generative Models, Uncertainty Quantification, and Physics-Motivated Optimization. The institute is led by Interim Director Mike Williams and Interim Deputy Director Phiala Shanahan, with founding Director Jesse Thaler currently on sabbatical. IAIFI actively cultivates talent through its Fellowship Program, annual Summer School for early-career researchers, and various educational initiatives, while building a dynamic AI+physics community through colloquia, workshops, and public engagement activities.

entities.description: [Alignment Research Center (ARC)] The Alignment Research Center (ARC) is a nonprofit research institute based in Berkeley, California, founded in April 2021 by former OpenAI researcher Paul Christiano. It focuses on aligning advanced artificial intelligence with human values through theoretical and empirical research, including mechanistic interpretability and formal verification. Notably, ARC evaluated GPT-4 for OpenAI in 2023, discovering it could hire humans via deception to bypass CAPTCHAs. The center operates as a 501(c)(3) charity and has expanded into policy work and industry collaborations. In December 2023, its evaluation team spun out as METR, an independent nonprofit.

entities.name: The Wistar Institute of Anatomy and Biology
entities.description: The Wistar Institute of Anatomy and Biology, founded in 1892 by Civil War Brigadier General Isaac Jones Wistar in memory of his great-uncle Dr. Caspar Wistar, is America's first independent biomedical research facility located in University City, Philadelphia. Named after Dr. Caspar Wistar, who authored the first American anatomy textbook and served as president of the American Philosophical Society after Thomas Jefferson, the Institute began as an anatomical teaching museum but evolved into a world leader in cancer, immunology, and infectious disease research. Wistar has been a National Cancer Institute-designated cancer center since 1972 and has developed groundbreaking vaccines including rubella (1969), rabies (1970s), and rotavirus (2016), as well as creating the Wistar rat (1908-1910), the first standardized laboratory animal from which over half of all lab rats today are descended. The Institute currently employs approximately 300 staff members including 130 doctoral-level scientists across 40+ laboratories, and in 2024 was ranked in the 1st percentile for innovation by SCImago Institution Ranking while receiving over $25 million in NIH funding.

entities.name: Texas defeats Boston College in Record-breaking fashion
entities.description: This College Baseball Daily blog post from May 31, 2009, provides contemporary coverage of the longest game in NCAA baseball history between Texas and Boston College. The article details the record-breaking 25-inning marathon where Texas won 3-2 after 7 hours and 3 minutes of play. Key highlights include Austin Wood's extraordinary 13-inning relief performance where he struck out 14 batters and kept Boston College hitless for 12.1 consecutive innings. The post comprehensively lists the multiple NCAA records set during the game: 42 combined strikeouts, 222 total chances, 69 assists, 192 plate appearances, and 171 at-bats. Individual records included Travis Tucker and Michael Torres each setting the NCAA single-game record with 12 at-bats, while Preston Clark recorded 33 putouts. The article notes that both closers - Wood and Boston College's Mike Belfiore - combined for 22.2 innings and 298 pitches in an unprecedented pitching duel.

entities.name: Efficacy and Safety of Deucravacitinib (BMS-986165) in Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis: Results from a Phase 2 Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
entities.description: This landmark 2018 NEJM paper by Papp et al. presents the Phase 2 trial of BMS-986165 (deucravacitinib), an oral selective TYK2 inhibitor, in 267 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The study randomized patients to multiple dosing regimens (3 mg twice daily, 6 mg twice daily, 12 mg once daily) or placebo for 12 weeks. At week 12, PASI 75 responses were 7% for placebo versus 39%, 69%, and 75% for deucravacitinib 3 mg BID, 6 mg BID, and 12 mg QD, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The most common adverse events included nasopharyngitis and headache; no herpes zoster, opportunistic infections, or major adverse cardiovascular events were reported. The trial established deucravacitinib's efficacy and safety profile, supporting its progression to Phase 3 trials and eventual FDA approval for psoriasis. [41][42]

entities.name: Bioluminescent Art Installations: Illuminating the Hidden Costs of Ocean Pollution
entities.description: Published on an environmental awareness platform, this article explores how bioluminescent art installations serve as powerful mediums for protesting ocean pollution. It details specific case studies like "Plastic Tides"—an installation using plastic bottles filled with bioluminescent algae that glow when disturbed but fade as organisms stress, symbolizing ecosystem disruption. Another project, "Chemical Glow," employs genetically modified jellyfish that emit light in response to water toxins, visualizing hidden marine dangers. The piece examines the scientific process behind bioluminescence (luciferin-luciferase reactions), artistic techniques (living organisms, artificial triggers, hybrid materials), and ethical considerations in using marine life for activism. It emphasizes how these installations transform polluted sites into immersive experiences that bridge art, science, and environmental advocacy.

entities.name: Ibn Yunus
entities.description: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi al-Said 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn Yunus ibn Abd al-'Ala al-Sadafi al-Misri (c. 950 - June 6, 1009) was an Egyptian astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer who worked during the Fatimid Caliphate. Born in Fustat, Egypt, to a family of scholars (his father was a noted historian), Ibn Yunus became perhaps the greatest astronomer of medieval Islam and the most important astronomer of medieval Egypt. His major work, al-Zij al-Kabir al-Hakimi (The Great Hakimi Tables), was a monumental astronomical handbook containing highly accurate observations of 40 planetary conjunctions and 30 lunar eclipses, with calculations accurate to the seventh decimal place. The Fatimid caliphs al-Aziz Billah and al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah supported his work, building him an observatory on Mount Mokattam near Fustat. Ibn Yunus made significant advances in trigonometry, being the first to establish laws for spherical trigonometry that converted multiplication operations into addition operations. Known as an eccentric who dressed shabbily and appeared absent-minded, he famously predicted his own death seven days in advance and died on the predicted day in 1009. His astronomical observations were so precise that they were used centuries later by Richard Dunthorne and Simon Newcomb in their calculations of the secular acceleration of the Moon, and a lunar crater bears his name.

entities.name: Royal Sea Bathing Infirmary (Royal Sea Bathing Hospital)
entities.description: The Royal Sea Bathing Infirmary, later known as the Royal Sea Bathing Hospital, was founded in 1791 by Dr. John Coakley Lettsom, a Quaker physician and philanthropist, in Margate, Kent, England. This pioneering medical institution was established specifically to treat scrofulous poor from London and is considered one of the earliest—if not the earliest—specialist orthopaedic hospitals in the UK. The hospital was revolutionary for its time, pioneering open-air treatment for patients with non-pulmonary tuberculosis through the therapeutic use of sunshine, fresh air, and sea bathing. The original building, designed by Revd. John Pridden between 1793-1796, featured colonnades and verandas where patients slept outdoors year-round, anticipating modern open-air treatment methods by over a century. The hospital expanded significantly in 1880 with a £30,000 donation from Sir Erasmus Wilson, adding new wards, a heated indoor salt-water pool, and a chapel. At its peak, the hospital accommodated 250 patients but faced financial challenges, eventually closing in the early 1990s when services moved to Thanet District Hospital. The Grade II listed complex has since been converted into luxury apartments, preserving its architectural heritage while ending its medical legacy that spanned over 200 years.

entities.name: Panavision International, L.P. v. Toeppen
entities.description: Panavision International, L.P. v. Toeppen (141 F.3d 1316) is a landmark 1998 Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion that addressed novel issues of personal jurisdiction and trademark dilution in cyberspace. The case involved defendant Dennis Toeppen registering domain names using Panavision's trademarks (panavision.com and panaflex.com) and demanding $13,000 to release them. The court affirmed that Toeppen's conduct constituted commercial use under the Federal Trademark Dilution Act of 1995, establishing that registering famous trademarks as domain names for extortion purposes dilutes the marks' distinctiveness. The ruling applied the "effects doctrine" to uphold California's personal jurisdiction over Toeppen, who operated from Illinois, setting crucial precedent for early internet trademark law and cybersquatting cases.

entities.name: The Vertical Earth Kilometer
entities.description: The Vertical Earth Kilometer is a permanent land art installation created by Walter De Maria in 1977, located in Friedrichsplatz Park in Kassel, Germany, in front of the Fridericianum museum. The artwork consists of a solid brass rod measuring exactly one kilometer (3,280.84 feet) in length and 5 centimeters (2 inches) in diameter, weighing 18 tons, which is inserted vertically into the ground with only its circular top flush with the earth's surface. The visible portion is surrounded by a two-by-two-meter red sandstone square, and remarkably, the installation has no plaque or marker identifying it as artwork. Commissioned for documenta 6 and funded by the Dia Art Foundation, the piece cost 750,000 Deutsche Marks (approximately $2 million in 2016) and took 79 days to install, requiring drilling through six geological layers. The Vertical Earth Kilometer serves as a companion piece to De Maria's 1979 work The Broken Kilometer in New York, which uses an identical brass rod divided into 500 segments displayed in a gallery setting. The installation exemplifies Minimalism, Conceptual Art, and Land Art movements, inviting viewers to question what lies beneath the surface of everyday reality.

entities.name: Armagh Observatory and Planetarium
entities.description: Armagh Observatory and Planetarium (AOP) is Ireland's leading centre for astronomical research and education, comprising two historically significant institutions. The Observatory was established in 1790 by Archbishop Richard Robinson, making it the oldest scientific institution in Northern Ireland and the longest continuously operating astronomical research institute in the UK and Ireland. The adjacent Planetarium was founded in 1968 by Dr. Eric Lindsay, the Observatory's seventh Director, and is the oldest operating planetarium in the UK and Ireland. The unified organization hosts around 25 astronomers and maintains an unbroken meteorological record dating back to 1794, earning it recognition as a Centennial Observing Station by the World Meteorological Organisation. entities.name: Hubble finds first galaxy in the local Universe without dark matter
entities.description: This ESA/Hubble science release from March 28, 2018, announces the groundbreaking discovery of NGC 1052-DF2, an ultra-diffuse galaxy located 65 million light-years away that appears to contain little to no dark matter—contradicting standard galaxy formation theories. The international research team, led by Yale's Pieter van Dokkum, used Hubble and ground-based observatories to determine the galaxy's size (larger than the Milky Way) and its stellar mass (250 times fewer stars than our galaxy). By measuring the velocities of 10 globular clusters, they found a velocity dispersion indicating at least 400 times less dark matter than expected for a galaxy of its type. The article features van Dokkum's famous quote about the galaxy being a "see-through galaxy" and discusses how this finding challenges alternative theories like Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). The release includes detailed notes on the methodology, a full list of collaborating institutions, and links to the Nature paper and supplementary images.

entities.name: Yi Sang (이상)
entities.description: Kim Haegyŏng (1910–1937), known by his pen name Yi Sang, was a Korean avant-garde writer, poet, architect, and painter during the Japanese colonial period. He graduated first in his class from Gyeongseong Technical College in 1928 with a degree in architecture and worked as a public official for the Government-General of Korea before contracting tuberculosis in 1933. Despite his short life of only 26 years, Yi Sang produced groundbreaking works that were initially rejected as incomprehensible, with his most famous poem series *Crow's Eye View* (1934) being called "the sleep talk of a lunatic" by contemporaries. His experimental writing incorporated scientific symbols, mathematical diagrams, homophonic wordplay, and visual elements, making him a pivotal yet controversial figure in modern Korean literature who was also a member of the literary group Guinhoe (League of Nine).

Using data sourced from the Central Bank of Nigeria's 2011 statistical bulletin, the research reveals that stock market capital significantly influences capital formation alongside other macroeconomic factors. The paper includes comprehensive chapters on theoretical frameworks, empirical literature, research methodology, and econometric analysis, culminating in recommendations for financial sector liberalization and increased public participation in stock exchange activities.

entities.name: Highsmith, Patricia | Strangers on a Train, an extraordinary association copy
entities.description: This auction lot offered a first edition of Patricia Highsmith's debut novel "Strangers on a Train" (1950) at Sotheby's December 2023 Fine Books and Manuscripts auction, estimated at $12,000-$18,000. The extraordinary association copy was the file copy of her literary agent Margot Johnson, featuring her stamp and presentation inscription to actress and aviator Ruth Chatterton dated January 1951. The timing is significant - inscribed just before Highsmith traveled to Europe to work on "The Price of Salt" and five months before Hitchcock's film adaptation. The catalog reveals that both Highsmith and Chatterton were clients of Johnson, described as a "notorious lesbian and a drunk," and that Highsmith recorded in her diaries discussing the pseudonym "Claire Morgan" for her lesbian-themed novel during a January 25, 1951 meeting with Johnson. The copy likely remained with Johnson's agency rather than reaching Chatterton, making it a rare early presentation copy from the year of publication.

entities.name: Chris Rainier: Investigating the Adapted Guitars of Harry Partch
entities.description: This detailed blog post from Fretboard Journal documents musician Chris Rainier's decade-long journey (2013-2023) recreating Harry Partch's three microtonal "Adapted Guitars." The article provides specific technical details: Partch first experimented in the 1940s on a 1928 Martin O-18K, while Rainier's replicas include a 1977 Takamine F-340 (Adapted Guitar 1) with six strings in three octave pairs tuned to Eb-G-B, a modified 1976 Takamine F-400 12-string converted to 10-string lap steel (Adapted Guitar 2), and a 1981 Takamine F-340 fretless lap steel (Adapted Guitar 3). Rainier collaborated with guitarist John Schneider, who was previously the only person with a replica, and recently released the album "Sorrowful Songs of the Silverswords" featuring these instruments. The post includes historical context about Partch's modifications between 1934-1942, including his innovation of inserting high stainless-steel frets into brass plates to achieve just intonation tuning.

entities.name: the McKay-Thompson series
entities.description: This blog post, published on March 22, 2008 by mathematician Lieven Le Bruyn, documents the precise moment when "Monstrous moonshine was born (sometime in 1978)" when John McKay realized that the linear term 196884 in the j-function expansion j(q) = q^-1 + 744 + 196884q + 21493760q² + 864229970q³ + ... was "surprisingly close" to the dimension of the smallest non-trivial irreducible representation of the monster group (196883). The post provides the exact mathematical relationships: 196884 = 1 + 196883, 21493760 = 1 + 196883 + 21296876, and 864229970 = 2×1 + 2×196883 + 21296876 + 842609326, revealing how the j-function coefficients correspond to linear combinations of monster group representation dimensions. The author also discusses how Richard Borcherds later explained these numerical facts through the graded representation V = ⊕i Vi of the Monster-group, where the dimension of the i-th factor Vi equals the coefficient in the j-function, leading to the McKay-Thompson series - modular functions known as Hauptmoduln discovered by John Conway.

entities.name: CFTC's Action Against Ooki DAO: A Landmark Case for Crypto Regulation
entities.description: This comprehensive legal analysis by Sasha Hodder, published May 7, 2024, examines the unprecedented CFTC enforcement action against Ooki DAO, treating it as an "unincorporated association" under the Commodity Exchange Act. The article details how the CFTC served the DAO through an online forum post—a novel approach that bypassed traditional service methods. It critically analyzes the questionable legal basis for classifying Ooki DAO as an unincorporated association, potentially exposing all token holders who voted on governance to liability. Hodder explores the regulatory implications, citing Commissioner Mersinger's dissent that the CFTC improperly applied state contract/tort case precedents to impose federal penalties without due process. The analysis covers the DAO's transition from bZeroX, the founders' comments about becoming "enforcement proof," and the chilling effect on DAO participation. With approximately 1,500 words of detailed legal commentary, this obscure blog post provides unique insights into the procedural innovations and regulatory overreach concerns surrounding this landmark case that resulted in a $643,542 penalty and permanent shutdown order against Ooki DAO.

entities.name: Tirzepatide versus insulin glargine in type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk (SURPASS-4): a randomised, open-label, parallel-group, multicentre, phase 3 trial
entities.description: Published in The Lancet on November 13, 2021, this phase 3 SURPASS-4 trial evaluated tirzepatide versus insulin glargine in 2,002 adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk across 187 sites in 14 countries. The study found tirzepatide 10 mg and 15 mg achieved superior HbA1c reductions (–2.43% and –2.58% respectively) versus glargine (–1.44%), meeting non-inferiority margins. Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea 12–23%, diarrhea 13–22%) were more common with tirzepatide, while hypoglycemia occurred less frequently (6–9% vs 19%). Crucially, adjudicated MACE-4 events showed no excess cardiovascular risk with tirzepatide (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.51–1.08). This was the first long-term cardiovascular safety assessment of a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist in a high-risk population, with funding from Eli Lilly.

entities.name: Olga Aleksandrovna Ladyzhenskaya
entities.description: Olga Aleksandrovna Ladyzhenskaya (1922–2004) was a pioneering Russian mathematician renowned for her groundbreaking work in partial differential equations, fluid dynamics, and the finite-difference method for the Navier-Stokes equations. Born in Kologriv, she overcame personal tragedy—her father was executed in 1937 as an "enemy of the people"—to become one of the most influential mathematicians of her era. Ladyzhenskaya authored over 200 scientific publications, including six monographs, and provided the first rigorous proofs for the convergence of finite difference methods for Navier-Stokes equations. She was shortlisted for the 1958 Fields Medal and received prestigious awards such as the Lomonosov Gold Medal (2002) and the John von Neumann Prize (1998). Her legacy includes mentoring notable students like Vladimir Faddeev and Nina Uraltseva, and her work continues to shape modern mathematical physics.

entities.name: Gabapentin for intractable hiccups in a patient undergoing peritoneal dialysis
entities.description: This is a 2008 case report published in Peritoneal Dialysis International, documenting successful treatment of intractable hiccups with gabapentin in a peritoneal dialysis patient. The report details dosing strategies, clinical response, and highlights gabapentin's rapid onset of action and favorable safety profile in renal impairment. It provides one of the earliest systematic evaluations of gabapentin specifically for dialysis-related intractable hiccups, with subsequent citation in 6 other publications. The case contributes to the limited evidence base for pharmacologic interventions in persistent hiccups, a condition with few controlled trials due to its rarity.

entities.name: Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corporation Form 10-K (2005)
entities.description: The Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corporation Form 10-K for fiscal year 2005 provides comprehensive financial and operational data for one of North America's largest railroads. The corporation reported operating revenues of $13.0 billion, a 10% increase from 2004, driven by strong consumer and agricultural product shipments. Net income rose to $1.5 billion, up from $1.3 billion in 2004, reflecting improved operational efficiency and pricing power. Operating expenses totaled $9.8 billion, with railway fuel costs increasing by 23% due to rising diesel prices. The report details the company's 32,000-route-mile network spanning 28 states and two Canadian provinces, serving key economic sectors including coal, intermodal, agricultural, and industrial products. Notable investments included $1.7 billion in capital expenditures, primarily for infrastructure improvements and equipment acquisitions. The document also discusses the company's transition to BNSF Railway Company name in January 2005 and its ongoing legal proceedings, including several environmental and labor-related cases. This annual report represents the final full year of operation before Berkshire Hathaway's eventual acquisition of the company in 2010.

entities.name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
entities.description: Henrietta Swan Leavitt (1868-1921) was an American astronomer whose groundbreaking work at the Harvard College Observatory revolutionized our understanding of the cosmos. As one of the "Harvard Computers," she meticulously analyzed photographic plates and discovered the period-luminosity relationship for Cepheid variable stars in 1912, known as Leavitt's Law. This relationship established that a Cepheid's pulsation period is directly related to its intrinsic brightness, providing the first "standard candle" to measure astronomical distances beyond our galaxy. Her discovery enabled Edwin Hubble to prove the existence of other galaxies and later formulate Hubble's Law, fundamentally altering the scale of the known universe. Despite earning only $0.30 an hour and facing progressive hearing loss, Leavitt identified 2,400 variable stars and developed the Harvard Standard for photographic magnitudes, which was adopted internationally in 1913.

entities.name: "Museum of Bad Art" Dedham Branch Location Details
entities.description: The Museum of Bad Art (MOBA) Dedham branch was located at 580 Washington Street, Dedham, Massachusetts, inside the Dedham Community Theatre. This specific location housed approximately 25-35 pieces from MOBA's permanent collection, featuring works that were "too bad to be ignored" with subjects ranging from landscapes to portraits with notable technical flaws. The Dedham location was MOBA's first permanent gallery space, established in 1995, and operated as a free admission venue where visitors could view artworks like "Lucy in the Field with Flowers" and "Sunday on the Pot with George." The theatre setting created a unique juxtaposition where moviegoers could experience bad art before or after film screenings, with the gallery occupying the basement level of the historic 1927 theatre building.

entities.name: Forrest J Ackerman
entities.description: Forrest J Ackerman (1916–2008) was an American magazine editor, literary agent, and foundational figure in science fiction fandom, often called "Forry" or "The Ackermonster." He edited *Famous Monsters of Filmland* (1958–1983), co-created Vampirella, and represented authors like Ray Bradbury and Isaac Asimov. Ackerman coined the term "sci-fi" in 1954, won a Hugo Award in 1953 as "#1 Fan Personality," and housed a collection of 300,000 sci-fi and horror memorabilia in his "Ackermansion." He hosted over 50,000 fans at open houses and was posthumously inducted into the Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame.

entities.name: European Fireball Network
entities.description: The European Fireball Network is an international astronomy organization established in 1963 that operates a systematic camera network for observing bright meteors (bolides) across Central Europe. Based primarily in Germany and the Czech Republic, the network currently consists of at least 34 camera stations spanning Germany, Czech Republic, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Slovakia, and Austria, covering approximately 1,000,000 square kilometers with stations spaced about 100 kilometers apart. The network is jointly operated by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the Astronomical Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Ondřejov, producing about 10,000 images per year and documenting approximately 1,200 hours of clear sky observations annually. The network detects about 50 large meteors per year and has achieved significant scientific breakthroughs, including the first photographic recording of a meteorite with known solar system origin (the Příbram meteorite of 1959) and the detailed observation of the Neuschwanstein meteorite fall in 2002. Modern digital cameras can detect meteors brighter than absolute magnitude -2 and collect radiometric light curves for those brighter than magnitude -4, with all meteoroids larger than 5 grams being detected regardless of entry velocity.

entities.name: A General Paradigm for A.I. Search Procedures
entities.description: This influential paper from AAAI-82 presents a unified General Branch and Bound (GBB) formulation that encompasses previous search algorithms as special cases, including A*, AO*, Alpha-Beta, and B*. Authored by Dana S. Nau, Vipin Kumar, and Laveen Kanal from the University of Maryland, the 6-page work was supported by NSF Grants 7822159 ENG and MCS81-17391. The paper establishes that AI search procedures can be understood through three core functions: selection, splitting, and pruning, with the key innovation being the generalized dominance concept in pruning. The authors demonstrate how their formulation provides a theoretical foundation for understanding most heuristic search procedures developed in AI, showing that algorithms like A* can be rewritten as instantiations of their best-first GBB procedure.

entities.name: A foothold on history: 25 years later, Mark Henderson still remembered for role in Pats' 'Snowplow Game'
entities.description: This Boston Herald retrospective article, published on December 12, 2007 (the 25th anniversary of the game) by sports columnist Steve Buckley, provides extensive detail about the infamous 1982 Snowplow Game between the Patriots and Dolphins. The article debunks several myths about the event, including that it wasn't actually a snowplow but a John Deere tractor with a brush, Henderson was never incarcerated at MCI-Walpole, and the snowplow actually created an inconvenience rather than helping the kick. It includes personal interviews with Mark Henderson (then 49, living in Rhode Island as a construction worker), kicker John Smith, and Patriots owner Robert Kraft. The article reveals Henderson served 2.5 years for small-time burglaries, was on work-release in September 1982, and received the game ball after the Patriots' 3-0 victory. Notable details include Henderson's son Mark Jr. giving Kraft a bear hug during a 2001 reunion, and the fact that there were false rumors Henderson had died, leading to confusion when the real Mark Henderson contacted the team.

entities.name: Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI)
entities.description: Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) is the national research institute for mathematics and computer science in the Netherlands, founded in 1946 as the Mathematical Centre and renamed in 1983 to reflect its expanded focus on computer science [0][1][2]. Located at Amsterdam Science Park and part of the Dutch Research Council (NWO-I), CWI employs approximately 200 administrative staff and over 150 researchers from more than 25 nationalities, organized into 15 research groups focusing on four fundamental areas: Algorithms, Data & Intelligent Systems, Cryptography & Security, and Quantum Computing [0][1][8]. The institute has made groundbreaking contributions including the creation of the Python programming language by Guido van Rossum, development of the first Dutch computers (Electrologica X1 and X8), establishing Europe's first internet connection to NSFNET in 1988, and registering the first non-US country code top-level domain (.nl) in 1986 [1][2]. CWI has generated 26 spin-off companies including notable ventures like Data Distilleries (acquired by IBM), SIDN (.nl domain registrar), and MonetDB, while its researchers have received prestigious awards such as the Gödel Prize, Lanchester Prize, and Spinoza Prize [1][2].

entities.name: Harry Kalven Jr.
entities.description: Harry Kalven Jr. (1914-1974) was an American legal scholar and the Harry A. Bigelow Professor of Law at the University of Chicago Law School, regarded as one of the preeminent legal scholars of the 20th century. He made foundational contributions to tort law, constitutional law, and First Amendment scholarship, coauthoring the widely used torts textbook "Cases and Materials on Torts" and the pioneering empirical study "The American Jury" with Hans Zeisel. Kalven coined the term "heckler's veto" and chaired the committee that produced the influential 1967 Kalven Report on university neutrality in political matters. His notable legal work included successfully defending comedian Lenny Bruce in an obscenity case before the Illinois Supreme Court in 1964, and his posthumously published work "A Worthy Tradition: Freedom of Speech in America" became a classic in First Amendment law. The Law and Society Association annually awards the Harry J. Kalven Jr. Prize for empirical scholarship advancing research in law and society.

entities.name: Ely Eel Festival World Eel Throwing Competition
entities.description: The World Eel Throwing Competition is a quirky annual event held during Ely's Eel Festival in Cambridgeshire, England, celebrating the city's historical connection to eels. Held on the Saturday of the May Bank Holiday weekend, the competition takes place in Jubilee Gardens following a parade from Cross Green outside Ely Cathedral. Participants throw specially made toy eels (not real ones - originally socks filled with rice in tights) in two age categories: under 16s and over 16s. The world record stands at 17.7 meters, set by Simon J in 2013, while recent winners include Chris A (14.8m in 2019, over 16s) and Marius A (13m in 2019, under 16s). The competition is part of a larger three-day festival attracting 7,000-8,000 visitors, featuring eel-themed food, real eel displays by the Environment Agency, and various entertainment acts. Each hourly winner receives a certificate, with overall category winners receiving trophies.

entities.name: The College Student Who Decoded the Data Hidden in Inca Knots
entities.description: Published on December 14, 2017, by Katherine Davis-Young on Atlas Obscura, this article details how Harvard freshman Manny Medrano made an archaeological breakthrough during spring break 2016 by decoding six khipus from the 17th-century Santa River Valley region of Peru. Working with Professor Gary Urton's Harvard Khipu Database Project (started in 2002), which contains records of over 900 Inca khipus from museums worldwide, Medrano matched the knotted cords to a Spanish colonial census document. His analysis revealed that cord attachment methods corresponded to social status and string colors related to first names among the 132 people recorded. The findings, published in the peer-reviewed journal Ethnohistory with Medrano as first author (extremely rare for an undergraduate), represent the first detailed decoding of khipu meaning beyond general numerical understanding, potentially serving as a key to unlock the hundreds of other khipus in the database.

entities.name: The Grolier Club
entities.description: Founded in January 1884, the Grolier Club is the oldest existing bibliophilic society in North America, headquartered at 47 East 60th Street in New York City. Named for the Renaissance-era French bibliophile Jean Grolier, the club was founded by nine individuals, including Robert Hoe III and Theodore L. DeVinne, with an initial membership of 50. Its mission is to foster the literary study of the book arts, encompassing printing, binding, and illustration. The club maintains a specialized research library with one of North America's most extensive collections of book auction and bookseller catalogs, alongside archives of prominent collectors like Sir Thomas Phillipps. It hosts public exhibitions in its two galleries, such as a 1971 display of the newly-discovered Grolier Codex, a pre-Columbian Maya manuscript. The current clubhouse, designed by Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue, opened in 1917 and includes a unique simulation of a 17th-century New York Dutch taproom for its members. Over its history, the club has had 26 presidents, with Nancy K. Boehm currently serving a term from 2022 to 2026, and its honorary members have included figures like Franklin D. Roosevelt and typographer Hermann Zapf.

entities.name: The Annaghmakerrig Papers at the Tyrone Guthrie Centre: a history of people and place
entities.description: This comprehensive blog post, written by archivist Anna Hunter and published on November 12, 2019, provides a detailed exploration of the Annaghmakerrig Papers spanning three centuries of family history. The collection encompasses documents from the Guthrie, Power, and Moorhead families who inhabited Annaghmakerrig House, now the Tyrone Guthrie Centre. The post highlights specific archival treasures including an 1820 land sale advertisement listing tenants by name and age, rent books from 1892, and poignant annotations on family documents. Notably, it features Sir Tyrone Guthrie's 1947 letter describing visits to the Warsaw Ghetto and Oswiencim concentration camp, alongside everyday items like a manure spreader agreement that reveals his deep community connections. The archive contains approximately 40 volumes and 1,000 documents, tracing the estate's history from deeds dating back to 1667 through to the 20th century, embodying what the author describes as "the expression of affinity to place and the people in it."

entities.name: Jeff Grell
entities.description: Jeff Grell is a pioneering figure in snowboarding, best known as the inventor of the highback binding—a transformative innovation that enabled more responsive control and helped launch modern snowboard equipment design. Starting as a Snurfer rider in 1968, he developed the first prototype called Hibaks in 1983, then collaborated with Tom Sims at Sims Snowboards to create the industry-standard convertible highback binding by 1985. Despite not initially patenting his invention due to lack of funds, he was later granted U.S. Patent No. 6,123,342 in 2000. Grell also contributed as an early competitor, event organizer, technical delegate, and the first Director of Snowboarding for Aspen Ski Company. In 2024, he was inducted into the Legends of Tahoe Snowboard Hall of Fame for his profound and lasting impact on the sport.

entities.name: David L. Waltz
entities.description: David Leigh Waltz (1943–2012) was a pioneering American computer scientist whose 1972 MIT dissertation on constraint propagation founded a critical field in artificial intelligence, enabling computers to infer 3D structures from 2D line drawings with shadows. Over his career, he held key positions including Professor at the University of Illinois (1973–1984), Director of Advanced Information Systems at Thinking Machines Corporation (1984–1993), President of NEC Research Institute (2000–2002), and Director of Columbia University's Center for Computational Learning Systems (2003–2012). He co-invented memory-based reasoning, contributed to massively parallel AI, and served as AAAI president (1997–1999), authoring over 100 publications and 3 edited volumes. He was a Fellow of both AAAI (1990) and ACM (1998), received the AAAI Distinguished Service Award (2011), and mentored 17 Ph.D. students, including notable AI researchers Tim Finin and Jordan Pollack.
