entities.name: Mount Lemmon SkyCenter
entities.description: The Mount Lemmon SkyCenter, part of the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory, is an astronomical research and public outreach facility located at 9,157 feet on Mount Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains. Established in 2008, it operates under a U.S. Forest Service permit and features the Schulman Telescope—a 32-inch Ritchey-Chrétien reflector and the largest dedicated public telescope in the Southwest. The site has a rich history, originally serving as a Cold War radar station (1956–1969) before transitioning to astronomical use by Steward Observatory in 1970. The SkyCenter offers flagship programs like SkyNights (5-hour public stargazing sessions for up to 28 participants, priced at $85 for adults) and AstronomerNights (private overnight telescope access), alongside workshops and educational camps. It hosts nine telescopes across Mount Lemmon and nearby Mount Bigelow, including instruments used by the Catalina Sky Survey, which scans over 800 square degrees nightly to detect near-Earth objects. The facility emphasizes interdisciplinary science education, combining astronomy with the unique "sky island" ecosystem of the region.

entities.name: Mystery of Overnight Returns — Deeper Look into Suspicious Stock Market Pattern
entities.description: Published on September 9, 2024, by Jakub Polec on Medium, this 5-minute read explores the overnight return anomaly where nearly all positive returns in major equity indices have occurred overnight over the past three decades. The article presents Python code for calculating overnight returns using the formula: Overnight Return = (Today's Adjusted Open / Yesterday's Adjusted Close) - 1, and applies Principal Component Analysis revealing that PC1 explains approximately 70% of variance in overnight returns across asset classes. The analysis covers broad market ETFs (SPY, QQQ), precious metals (GLD, SLV, PALL), tech giants like Apple, and European stocks, showing consistent overnight outperformance except in bonds (TLT) where intraday returns dominate. The post has generated 126 reads and includes interactive plots comparing cumulative overnight versus intraday returns across different assets.

entities.name: A machine learning model to identify shipwrecks in underwater archaeology research
entities.description: Leila Character, a doctoral student in geography at the University of Texas at Austin, has developed an AI model capable of recognizing wrecks on the seafloor with 92% accuracy. The system uses photographs taken by ships and aerial images to identify underwater debris, trained using tens of thousands of images from NOAA's data records of known shipwrecks. The imagery extends up to 23 kilometers off the coast and reaches a depth of 85 meters. This collaborative project between the University of Texas and the US Navy's Underwater Archaeology Subdivision was published by researchers including Agustin Ortiz of the US Navy's Marine Archaeology Branch, Sheryl Luzzadder-Beach, and Tim Beach. The research team aims to expand the model globally and develop customizable machine learning systems for various archaeological conditions, with potential applications for finding both military and civilian vessel wrecks.

entities.name: How Balkan 'folk dances' are made – "Arranged Folklore"
entities.description: Published on folkdancefootnotes.org, this ethnographic blog post explores the transformation of Balkan folk dances from traditional village practices to state-managed performances after WWII. The author details how pre-war dances were spontaneous, social events lasting 10+ minutes with live music, contrasting them with post-war Communist-era 'arranged folklore' that stripped dances of religious elements and standardized choreography for state propaganda. The post cites Yvonne Hunt's Traditional Dance in Greek Culture and Mirjana Laušević's Balkan Fascination, describing how dances evolved from organic community expressions to political tools. It identifies two fundamental Balkan dance patterns—Taproot dances and Uneven Walking—that form the basis of thousands of regional variations, with dances traditionally passed down through generations rather than created. The blog includes 5+ internal links to related ethnographic articles and analyzes how industrialization forced rural communities into urban settings, fundamentally altering dance's social function from spiritual communion to mechanical performance.

entities.name: SA 42 Samoa 14 - Rugby World Cup 1995 Quarter-final Match Data
entities.description: On 10 June 1995, South Africa defeated Western Samoa 42-14 in the Rugby World Cup quarter-final at Ellis Park, Johannesburg, with Chester Williams scoring a record four tries (20 points) and Gavin Johnson adding 12 points from conversions and penalties. The match featured an attendance of 50,000, was refereed by Jim Fleming (Scotland), and saw seven Springboks injured, including André Joubert with a broken hand. Samoa managed only two tries and two conversions, with captain François Pienaar leading South Africa's combined 128-test-cap starting lineup. This obscure digital match record, hosted on bokhist.com, provides granular team lists, player statistics, and historical context for the bruising encounter that propelled South Africa toward their eventual World Cup triumph.

entities.name: Olga Russakovsky
entities.description: Olga Russakovsky is a Ukrainian-American associate professor of computer science at Princeton University and a leading researcher in computer vision and machine learning. She is best known as one of the primary architects of the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, a pivotal project that accelerated the development of modern AI through its annual competition and massive dataset. Her 2015 PhD thesis, "Scaling Up Object Detection," was completed at Stanford University under the supervision of Fei-Fei Li. Beyond her technical contributions, Russakovsky is a prominent advocate for diversity and fairness in AI, co-founding the nonprofit AI4ALL in 2017 and establishing outreach programs like Stanford SAILORS (now Stanford AI4ALL) and Princeton AI4ALL to increase participation from underrepresented groups in artificial intelligence. Her research specifically addresses algorithmic bias, and she has been recognized with numerous awards, including being named to MIT Technology Review's "35 Innovators Under 35" in 2017 and receiving the Anita Borg Early Career Award in 2020.

entities.name: Cognitive Maps of Time and Tide Among Medieval Seafarers
entities.description: Published in the journal Man (Vol. 20, No. 2) in June 1985 by Charles O. Frake, this 17-page article examines how medieval sailors in northern Europe used the mariners' compass rose as a cognitive device to correlate lunar and solar time for predicting tides and currents. The study highlights their sophisticated mental models for memorizing tidal regimes at various ports, challenging assumptions about the cognitive abilities of non-literate societies. Frake argues that medieval seafarers demonstrated formal operational thinking, a cognitive level often mistakenly reserved for modern scientific minds, by solving complex tidal navigation challenges without written tables. The article has been cited 136 times, reflecting its significant impact on anthropological and historical studies of cognition and navigation.
